claims.text: The corrosion resistance of chemical-processing and nuclear-grade steels is controlled by a self-healing, chromium-rich passive oxide film.
The passive oxide film minimizes further corrosion by hindering diffusion of corrosive species.
Steels containing sufficient chromium naturally form a thin, adherent passive oxide layer during processing or minimal air exposure.
The corrosion-controlling surface structure is a coherent, uniformly distributed chromium oxide layer.
Chromium in the steel preferentially oxidizes upon environmental exposure.
Preferential chromium oxidation forms a passive surface layer.
The passive layer acts as a barrier against oxygen and aggressive ions.
The barrier lowers the rate of electrochemical reactions responsible for corrosion.
Samples retaining or rapidly re-forming the passive layer will have lower corrosion rates than samples where the layer is removed or its formation is inhibited.
Untreated steel samples develop a natural passive film under the test conditions.
Effective passivation requires chromium content above a critical threshold.
The proposed mechanism holds only in environments that do not severely disrupt passive-film stability.
The mechanism may not apply to lower-alloy steels or under extremely aggressive conditions.
Minor differences in composition, processing history, and environmental conditions can alter passive-film formation and corrosion-rate reduction.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis explicitly describes the film as self-healing and predicts protection when it quickly re-forms, but the falsification rule treats similar film reformation and corrosion behavior in etched and untreated samples as refutation. Similar behavior after rapid re-passivation could instead be consistent with the proposed self-healing mechanism.

The removed-film group is treated as the adverse comparator, although removal alone does not ensure that film formation remains inhibited during exposure. The intervention therefore does not cleanly maintain the mediator difference assumed by the prediction.
